questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x-16y)\,i+(x+y)\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x-16y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{cos}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi -0) \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i-2x\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={4}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $4.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2x=-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=8\,i-(x+3)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={2}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $2.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =8, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+3=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for sine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(16\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274301/assets/fbfe241043e9014c1b633d163cf7e06234db70702a9052297b5df8b9df3fd82f.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274301/assets/d432857e3350dfcb70a2a00b66ad9b86bc207382edd277c2169be0834c1710e0.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{t},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=\frac{1}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)-({t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}\frac{1}{t}+1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2)-(\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is given by $y={x}^{3}$ from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-3{x}^{2}\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274301/assets/1d54fe3c07f04a7d05567942e3eea6efaf1cb516070a5d7cc31ef726c0ddb423.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-3{x}^{2}=-3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3{t}^{2})\cdot (3{t}^{2})-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-9{t}^{4}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\frac{9{t}^{5}}{5}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{9}{5}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{14}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
